newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia begins spacewalk lessons for U.S. astronaut.
newsitem.headline: Russia begins spacewalk lessons for U.S. astronaut.

text.p: Russian space officials on Friday began training U.S. astronaut David Wolf for spacewalks outside the crippled Mir space station after he was abruptly told to stand in for the next mission.

"After the decision was taken we drew up the programme yesterday evening and began the training today," Boris Kryuchkov, the deputy director of Russia's Star City cosmonaut training centre outside Moscow, told Reuters.

On Wednesday, Wendy Lawrence, the U.S. astronaut originally intended to join Mir next month, told a news conference she was eager to fly. Hours later, NASA officials said they had decided to send her back-up, Wolf.

NASA said Lawrence did not fit into the Russian spacesuit and so could not perform spacewalks whereas Wolf, 40, a medical doctor and inventor, could. Russian space officials quickly devised a rigorous training programme to familiarise him with their suit and spacewalk procedures.

"In the coming days he will perform practical work in the suit, then in the hydro-laboratory, he'll fly in the Il-96 plane where we have zero gravity, and he'll work in two different pressure chambers with a suit," Kryuchkov said.
"Every exercise will be repeated several times, so he'll be sure about the lessons."

The ability to perform spacewalks has become important because Mir needs a series of repairs after it collided with its supply ship on June 25 in the worst accident of its 11-year history. It is now running on partial power.

Anatoly Solovyov and Pavel Vinogradov, the two Russian cosmonauts who will lead the repairs, left on Thursday for the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan ahead of their scheduled August 5 blast-off to Mir.
On August 20 they plan to re-attach cables to the solar panels in the damaged and airless Spektr module, a risky job that should restore additional power to Mir.

Wolf will blast off around September 28 on the U.S. space shuttle after he finishes his training in Star City, according to Frank Culbertson, who heads NASA's cooperation with the Russian space station.

Culbertson said on Thursday that Wolf had had about 150 hours of spacewalk training in the United States, although he has never performed an actual spacewalk. He flew on the space shuttle Columbia for 14 days in 1993.

During his Mir mission Wolf is expected to take at least one spacewalk to remove U.S. scientific equipment from Mir's exterior. But first he has to learn the distinct design features of the Russian suit.

"He must know how to use the spacesuit. With our spacesuits, you don't put it on, you enter it like an open door, and then close it," Kryuchkov said, adding that Wolf's private lessons would last at least a month.
"A spacesuit is like a little spaceship, with its own life support systems to regulate temperature, humidity, air-flow and pressure. The cosmonaut must know how to control all of these things."
Culbertson said Wolf may take additional spacewalks during his time aboard Mir if the need to assist his Russian crewmates arises.
